title: Finite-Sample ATE Frontier under Rough Confounding and Finite Conditional Outcome Moments
banked_reason: D0.5.G tier=subfield < floor=field; paper_score_ceiling 7.0 < 7.4; NOT salvageable in scope. Dedicated math referee passed with zero findings and all four citations verified; independent terminal validity gate confirms below-floor downgrade.
gap_reasons: The delivered matched rates settle the fixed one-dimensional public-uniform s=1/16, q=3/2 experiment; they do not establish a general smoothness–moment frontier or unknown-design attainment. The benchmark ratios compare different experiments, including the known-effective-density specialization of [Robins et al., Theorem 6.1](https://economics.yale.edu/sites/default/files/tchetgen_aos1515.pdf), and therefore do not establish a same-design bounded-versus-heavy-outcome phase transition. The public budget forces the estimator to zero and the interval to [-2,2] whenever floor(n/5)<2^105, so observable attainment does not supply practically usable precision at realistic sample sizes. The application discussion supplies motivation without delivered evidence overcoming this calibration limitation; fixed-parameter scope and impractical certificates constrain the projected paper score. The exact-frontier proof's reference to the preceding theorem as 'still-unproved' is stale, and the Poisson-affinity leaf needs an explicit citation and normalization mapping to [Leskelä, Theorem 5.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.00294#S5). [D0.5.G projected paper-score gate: paper_score_ceiling 7 < 7.4, so the graded tier 'field' is capped at 'subfield'. The score assesses the delivered research package without credit for unfinished work.]

This delivered mixed-contraction theorem is presented as a core novelty, but its node supplies no theorem-level comparison to the closest mixed-resolution/HOIF result class stating exactly what the heavy-leg contraction table newly permits; add that comparison and its significance at the theorem.
proof_attempt_summary: Discovery derived the fixed public-uniform one-dimensional ATE frontier with MSE order n^(-8/21) and honest interval length order n^(-4/21), including mixed-projection contractions and matching original-record converses. The final math referee passed with zero findings and four verified citations, but the authoritative tier was subfield with a 7.0 paper-score ceiling below the field threshold 7.4; bounded editorial repairs cannot lift it. Formalization was not entered: no Lean theorem or accepted result is claimed; broader scope or usable finite-sample calibration remains new research.
tldr: This paper solves the finite-sample original-record ATE frontier on the full public-uniform, positive-overlap, Holder-\(1/16\), conditional-\(3/2\)-moment class. It proves \(R_n\asymp n^{-8/21}\) and \(H_n\asymp n^{-4/21}\), with no logarithmic loss and \(H_n\asymp\sqrt{R_n}\). A total observable six-term reciprocal-correction estimator and public honest interval attain the rates, while a mirrored rare-mark complete-record experiment gives matching all-procedure converses. The mixed-contraction theorem isolates the interaction between heavy outcomes and rough propensity learning. Theorem 2 compares the resulting \(4/21\) precision exponent with the faster separate scalar finite-moment and bounded-response projection benchmarks. The class is new and informed by those sources and Jin--Syrgkanis; it is not claimed to equal or be included in their published model classes.
gap: Published projection corrections and robust scalar means address separate obstacles. Their inspected theorem classes do not determine the joint finite-moment rough-confounding ATE experiment. Fixed-law heavy-score inference does not give finite-sample honesty on its whole law class. The close Jin--Syrgkanis ATE minimax result uses a supplied-nuisance experiment; its scope differs along the dimensions stated in the literature comparison.
fill: The deliverable pairs a legal complete-likelihood converse with a total observable reciprocal-correction estimator and public finite-sample interval. The mixed-resolution contraction audit decides whether the provisional schedule works before any exact exponent or logarithm is chosen.
